hints: Think about how many shared pairs of electrons join the two N atoms in $\text{N}_2$ and what this means for bond polarity.
Link the strength of this bond to the energy needed to break it before nitrogen can react.
walkthrough:
Picture the bond holding nitrogen together**
Each nitrogen atom needs three more electrons to get a full outer shell, so the two atoms share three pairs of electrons. That gives you an N≡N triple bond, and because both atoms are identical the bond is completely non-polar with no dipole to attract other reagents.

Connect bond strength to reactivity**
A triple bond is very short and very strong. For nitrogen to react, that bond must first be broken, and breaking it needs a huge input of energy. At normal temperatures molecules do not have that energy, so $\text{N}_2$ stays inert.

Final answer: $\text{N}_2$ contains a very strong, non-polar N≡N triple bond.
A very large amount of energy is needed to break this bond, so nitrogen is unreactive.

hints: Count the outer electrons on one N atom (Group 15) and work out how many must be shared to give each N an octet.
walkthrough:
Count the outer electrons**
Nitrogen is in Group 15, so each N brings 5 outer electrons. To get an octet, each N must share 3 electrons, giving 6 electrons shared in total between the atoms.

Place the remaining electrons**
After sharing 3 each, each N has 2 electrons left over. Those sit as a lone pair on each N. In your diagram show three shared pairs in the middle using dots for one N and crosses for the other, plus one lone pair of dots on one N and one lone pair of crosses on the other.
Final answer: Dot-and-cross diagram showing N≡N with 6 shared electrons (3 bonding pairs) between the N atoms and one lone pair (2 non-bonding electrons) on each N atom. Each N has an octet.

hints: Recall from (a)(i) that the N≡N bond needs a huge energy input before reaction can start, then think what lightning supplies.
walkthrough:
See lightning as an energy source**
You already know $\text{N}_2$ will not react because breaking N≡N needs so much energy. Lightning is extremely hot and energetic. It gives the $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ molecules enough kinetic energy to overcome that high activation energy barrier, so $\text{N}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NO}$ can occur.
Final answer: Lightning provides the very high activation energy needed to break the strong N≡N bond and the $\text{O=O}$ bond.

hints: First think how colourless $\text{NO}$ is oxidised further in air by $\text{O}_2$ to give brown $\text{NO}_2$.
Then think how $\text{NO}_2$ dissolves in rainwater in the presence of $\text{O}_2$ to form $\text{HNO}_3$.
walkthrough:
Oxidise NO to NO2**
$\text{NO}$ made in the lightning strike reacts with more oxygen in the air. Each $\text{NO}$ picks up one O atom: $$\text{NO} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2} \rightarrow \text{NO}_{2}$$ Check atoms: one N and two O on each side, so it balances.

Dissolve NO2 to make nitric acid**
Nitrogen dioxide is an acidic gas. With rainwater and further oxygen it forms nitric acid: $$2\text{NO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{HNO}_{3}$$ This is how lightning leads naturally to nitrates falling in rain.

Final answer: 1: $\text{NO} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2} \rightarrow \text{NO}_{2}$
2: $2\text{NO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{HNO}_{3}$

hints: Start by thinking where soluble nitrates go when it rains heavily on fertilised fields.
Consider what extra nitrates in lakes and rivers do to the growth of algae and water plants, and what happens to light below the surface.
Follow what happens when that extra plant material dies, which organisms break it down, and what gas they use up.
walkthrough:
Get nitrates into water**
Nitrate fertilisers are very soluble in water. When farmers use too much, rain washes or leaches the excess off fields into rivers, lakes and groundwater. That suddenly enriches natural water with nutrients.

Grow too much algae**
Nitrates are plant food, so algae and surface plants grow explosively, forming an algal bloom. This thick layer blocks sunlight from reaching plants deeper down. Without light they cannot photosynthesise and they die, and then the algae also die. Bacteria feed on all this dead matter and decompose it.

Remove the oxygen**
Aerobic bacteria use dissolved oxygen for respiration as they decay the dead material. The oxygen concentration in the water drops sharply. Fish and other aquatic organisms cannot survive without enough dissolved oxygen, so animal and plant life is reduced. This whole sequence is eutrophication.

Final answer: Soluble nitrates are leached / washed into rivers and groundwater.
This causes an algal bloom which blocks sunlight, preventing photosynthesis by plants below, which then die. Bacteria decompose the dead organisms.
Decomposition uses up dissolved oxygen, so oxygen concentration falls and aquatic life dies.

hints: Recall whether calcium hydroxide is acidic or alkaline and what effect it will have on acidic soil.
walkthrough:
Treat soil like an acid**
Many soils become too acidic for healthy crops. Calcium hydroxide, $\text{Ca}(\text{OH})_{2}$, is a base. Adding it neutralises excess soil acidity, raising the $\text{pH}$ toward the optimum range for plant growth.
Final answer: To neutralise acidic soil / to raise / increase soil $\text{pH}$.

hints: Recall the standard test for the ammonium ion with a base: what pungent gas is released?
Think about why hydroxide ions can push this gas out of its salt, in terms of a stronger base displacing a weaker volatile base.
walkthrough:
Name the gas**
Whenever an ammonium salt is warmed with a base, ammonia is released: $$\text{NH}_{4}^{+} + \text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{NH}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ So the gas is $\text{NH}_{3}$.

Explain the displacement**
Hydroxide from $\text{Ca}(\text{OH})_{2}$ is a stronger base than ammonia. It takes a proton from $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$, displacing volatile $\text{NH}_{3}$ from the salt. That is why ammonium fertilisers should not be mixed with lime, or nitrogen is lost as ammonia.

Final answer: gas: ammonia, $\text{NH}_{3}$
explanation: hydroxide ions / base displaces $\text{NH}_{3}$ from $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$.

hints: Identify the reacting pair: a solid carbonate added to dilute nitric acid, what gas does this combination always give?
Think about what you would see happening to the solid carbonate and the solution as the gas escapes.
walkthrough:
Spot the carbonate plus acid reaction**
You have solid $\text{CaCO}_{3}$ going into dilute $\text{HNO}_{3}$. Carbonate plus acid always gives salt plus water plus carbon dioxide: $$\text{CaCO}_{3} + 2\text{HNO}_{3} \rightarrow \text{Ca}(\text{NO}_{3})_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$$ The $\text{CO}_{2}$ escapes as bubbles.

Describe only what you see**
Do not write the equation as your observation. State the visuals: vigorous fizzing or effervescence, and the white solid gradually disappears as soluble calcium nitrate forms.

Final answer: Effervescence / fizzing / bubbling (of $\text{CO}_{2}$).
Solid calcium carbonate disappears / dissolves.

hints: Recall the general pattern for heating a Group 2 nitrate: it gives the metal oxide plus nitrogen dioxide plus oxygen.
walkthrough:
Apply the Group 2 nitrate pattern**
All Group 2 nitrates decompose on heating in the same way: metal nitrate gives metal oxide plus nitrogen dioxide plus oxygen. For calcium: $$2\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_{3})_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{CaO} + 4\text{NO}_{2} + \text{O}_{2}$$ Check balance: 2 Ca, 4 N and 12 O on both sides.
